For the compression of durative actions, we give a criterion on the values that actions read, prove that compression is sound, and show that it is not complete, so its failure is never reported as a proof. An independent validator checks every plan. The engineering application is on-line task planning for robots: Kairos is open source, packaged for the Robot Operating System, and the default planner of a widely used planning framework. On 1,756 public tasks from nine suites, Kairos solves more tasks than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite within 100 milliseconds, 1 second and 30 seconds; it proves ten of eleven unsolvable tasks, and handles each of the seventeen language features probed, where no other planner handles more than eight.

articles.title: The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.39621v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.

articles.title: An Augmented Lagrangian Approach to Lifted Bellman Linear Programming
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14183v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Temporal-difference critics regress onto a bootstrapped target and usually need a target network. Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) instead expresses the in-sample optimal values of offline RL as the solution to a linear program over the dataset. Its neural solver ALBUM relaxes the constraints into hinge penalties with fixed coefficients, and its guarantees are conditions on coefficients chosen in advance. We solve the same program with the method of multipliers: the coefficients become multipliers learned by dual ascent, with one penalty parameter $\rho$. In the convex case the fixed points are the KKT pairs of LBLP, and at every stationary point the applied constraint weights balance the objective exactly. The critic can serve a Gaussian actor, a flow actor, and best-of-N sampling, and for the Gaussian actor we propose an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective. With a single $Q$ and $V$ and no target network, our AL-LBLP with best-of-N reaches 60.1\% average success on the 50 state-based OGBench tasks. On long-horizon tasks, it reaches 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant and 79.8% on antmaze-giant. It does not collapse up to batch size 8192.

articles.title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.15592v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3-82.0% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1-2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. Checkpoints trained further for embedding or reranking bring no gain. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.

articles.title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.17309v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.

articles.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.18543v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

articles.title: Controllable Chains of Thought Can Reveal Less, Even Without Evasion Training
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.21799v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

articles.title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.21832v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models likely outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification), while weaker models score near or below them. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

articles.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.22432v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

articles.title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.22897v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

articles.title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.23010v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

articles.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.23445v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

articles.title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.24254v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

articles.title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.24869v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

articles.title: Ensemble Logic
articles.summary:
arXiv:2408.14443v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We interpret formulas over metric monoids, that is, commutative monoids equipped with translation-invariant metrics. Displacement evaluates a formula at a translated point, while bounded existence and bounded universality evaluate it at some or every point of a window of prescribed length. Quantification over points and lengths allows the same variable to occur in the parameters of several operators. This provides a common framework for temporal and spatial reasoning in discrete, dense and multi-dimensional settings. Our main result establishes a sharp undecidability boundary for satisfiability over the natural numbers: satisfiability is undecidable already for formulas $\exists N\,\exists n\,\Psi$ in which $\Psi$ is built from the letters of a fixed alphabet by conjunction, disjunction, displacement and bounded universality. We prove this by a reduction from Post's Correspondence Problem. We also present results, in part from companion work, that place this theorem in the general theory of EL. These include an atomic-displacement normal form for covariant windows and composition laws for discrete and dense time. The discrete logic admits an embedding of linear temporal logic, defines the accepting runs of every B\"uchi automaton, and has a sound equational calculus. For the rational logic, we show that every fixed formula can be evaluated in polynomial time on interval models in which atomic propositions are interpreted by finite unions of intervals. Finally, we represent timed words over positions and real time and compare two window geometries; with rectangular windows, two shared lengths yield undecidability on finite timed words.

articles.title: FlexTSF: A Flexible Forecasting Model for Time Series with Variable Regularities
articles.summary:
arXiv:2410.23160v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generalizing across time series with irregular temporal structures poses a persistent challenge for universal time series forecasting models. Existing approaches often assume regular sampling or depend heavily on imputation, which limits their applicability in real-world scenarios where irregularities are prevalent due to diverse sensing devices and recording practices. To address this gap, we propose FlexTSF, a flexible and domain-adaptive forecasting model specifically designed for time series with variable temporal regularities. At its foundation lies the IVP Patcher, a continuous-time patching module leveraging Initial Value Problems (IVPs) to inherently handle uneven sampling intervals, variable sequence lengths, and missing values. Built upon a decoder-only Transformer architecture, FlexTSF integrates normalized timestamp inputs and domain-specific statistical descriptors through a specialized causal self-attention mechanism, enabling adaptability across domains. Extensive experiments on 16 datasets demonstrate FlexTSF's effectiveness, significantly outperforming existing models in classic forecasting scenarios, zero-shot generalization, and low-resource fine-tuning conditions.

articles.title: CP-Guard+: A New Paradigm for Malicious Agent Detection and Defense in Collaborative Perception
articles.summary:
arXiv:2502.07807v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Collaborative perception (CP) is a promising method for safe connected and autonomous driving, which enables multiple vehicles to share sensing information to enhance perception performance. However, compared with single-vehicle perception, the openness of a CP system makes it more vulnerable to malicious attacks that can inject malicious information to mislead the perception of an ego vehicle, resulting in severe risks for safe driving. To mitigate such vulnerability, we first propose a new paradigm for malicious agent detection that effectively identifies malicious agents at the feature level without requiring verification of final perception results, significantly reducing computational overhead. Building on this paradigm, we introduce CP-GuardBench, the first comprehensive dataset provided to train and evaluate various malicious agent detection methods for CP systems. Furthermore, we develop a robust defense method called CP-Guard+, which enhances the margin between the representations of benign and malicious features through a carefully designed Dual-Centered Contrastive Loss (DCCLoss). Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on both CP-GuardBench and V2X-Sim, and demonstrate the superiority of CP-Guard+.

articles.title: LLM-Based Threat Detection and Prevention Framework for IoT Ecosystems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2505.00240v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced complex and evolving cybersecurity challenges. This paper presents a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework for intelligent threat detection and prevention in IoT networks. The proposed architecture integrates two core components: a Detection Component that leverages fine-tuned models trained on IoT-specific datasets (IoT-23 and TON_IoT) to identify anomalous network behaviours, and a Prevention Component that generates adaptive response strategies to mitigate detected threats. The framework incorporates prompt management, local adaptation, and global refinement modules to support context-aware decision-making and continuous model-guided adaptation. Experimental validation in a Docker-based edge-cloud environment shows that BERT Small achieves 99.75% accuracy, F1-score, precision, and recall for threat detection, while the Prevention LLM achieves 98.3% accuracy in selecting suitable mitigation actions. These results highlight the potential of LLM-driven architectures to provide explainable and adaptive security solutions for next-generation IoT ecosystems.

articles.title: AudioTurbo: Fast Text-to-Audio Generation with Rectified Diffusion
articles.summary:
arXiv:2505.22106v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diffusion models have significantly improved the quality and diversity of text-to-audio (TTA) generation but are hindered by slow inference speed. Recent flow-based approaches have been explored for accelerating TTA generation. However, these approaches typically rely on dedicated flow-based generative frameworks and do not directly exploit existing pre-trained diffusion-based TTA models. To address this limitation while leveraging the strong generative capabilities of pre-trained diffusion models, we integrate rectified diffusion into these models to improve TTA generation efficiency. Specifically, we propose AudioTurbo, which learns first-order approximate ordinary differential equation (ODE) paths from deterministic noise-sample pairs generated by a pre-trained TTA model. Experiments show that our approach outperforms a flow-matching-based acceleration model in both generation quality and inference speed.

articles.title: A Quasi-experimental Study of Conversational AI-supported Engagement in Large CS Courses
articles.summary:
arXiv:2506.18941v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Lucrative career prospects and creative opportunities often attract students to enroll in computer science courses, resulting in large class sizes. A common challenge in large classrooms is the lack of engagement between students and both the instructor and the learning material. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) present an opportunity to leverage Conversational Artificial Intelligence (CAI) to address this challenge. To examine the potential of CAI to support engagement with learning material, we designed an in class activity in a large Software Engineering course in which students interacted with a CAI tool. Using a quasi-experimental, within-subject study design in a real classroom at a large public United States University. We compared student engagement during an activity that involved the use of CAI for discussion with an activity that did not (peer discussion). For our analysis, we collected data on students interactions with the CAI tool and their self-reported responses on multiple engagement scales. Results show higher student engagement with the learning material in the activity involving CAI discussion as opposed to without (peer discussion). Higher self-reported learning was also observed in the activity with CAI as compared to without. Students also reported significantly more usefulness for learning in the CAI condition. Overall, our results indicate that CAI (ChatGPT) has the potential to support engagement with learning content during in-class activities in large class sizes.

articles.title: FlowDrive: moderated flow matching with data balancing for trajectory planning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2509.21961v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Learning-based planners are sensitive to the long-tailed distribution of driving data. Common maneuvers dominate datasets, while dangerous or rare scenarios are sparse. This imbalance can bias models toward the frequent cases and degrade performance on critical scenarios. To tackle this problem, we compare balancing strategies for sampling training data and find reweighting by trajectory pattern an effective approach. We then present FlowDrive, a flow-matching trajectory planner that learns a conditional rectified flow to map noise directly to trajectory distributions with few flow-matching steps. We further introduce moderated, in-the-loop guidance that injects small perturbation between flow steps to systematically increase trajectory diversity while remaining scene-consistent. On nuPlan and the interaction-focused interPlan benchmarks, FlowDrive achieves state-of-the-art results among learning-based planners and approaches methods with rule-based refinements. After adding moderated guidance and light post-processing (FlowDrive*), it achieves overall state-of-the-art performance across nearly all benchmark splits. Our code is available at https://github.com/einsteinguang/flow_drive_planner.

articles.title: Rhythm-TTS: High-Fidelity Shortcut Latent Modeling and Probabilistic Rhythm Generation for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.02848v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) systems are commonly built on either discrete codec tokens or continuous acoustic representations. Discrete-token models benefit from stable sequence modeling and explicit speech factorization, but they ultimately synthesize speech through codebook lookup and codeword composition, which can accumulate errors and impose a quality ceiling on naturalness and speaker similarity. Continuous-representation models can generate fine-grained speech latents directly, but often require heavier in-context modeling and less explicit alignment. This paper presents \textbf{Rhythm-TTS}, a shortcut zero-shot TTS framework that combines the factorizability of discrete codec tokens with the fidelity of continuous latent generation. Instead of using predicted codec tokens as the final acoustic representation, Rhythm-TTS uses them as a semantic-acoustic prior and directly generates holistic continuous speech latents with flow matching, bypassing the discrete-to-latent reconstruction path at inference time. We further address an underexplored dimension of speech naturalness: rhythm diversity across multiple synthesis runs. Motivated by the hypothesis that rhythm variation is largely governed by phoneme duration changes and the occurrence of silent pauses, we introduce probabilistic Duration and Silence Generators to sample dynamic pacing patterns before acoustic generation. Experiments on zero-shot TTS benchmarks evaluate intelligibility, naturalness, speaker similarity, efficiency, and run-to-run rhythm diversity, showing that the proposed shortcut latent modeling and probabilistic rhythm generation improve the fidelity and temporal naturalness of non-autoregressive zero-shot TTS. Code and audio samples are available at our demo page https://rhythm-tts.github.io.

articles.title: Predicting Public Health Impacts of Electricity Usage
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.22031v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The electric power sector is a leading source of air pollutant emissions, impacting the public health of nearly every community. Although regulatory measures have reduced air pollutants, fossil fuels remain a significant component of the energy supply, highlighting the need for more advanced demand-side approaches to reduce the public health impacts. To enable health-informed demand-side management, we introduce HealthPredictor, a domain-specific AI model that provides an end-to-end pipeline linking electricity use to public health outcomes. The model comprises three components: a fuel mix predictor that estimates the contribution of different generation sources, an air quality converter that models pollutant emissions and atmospheric dispersion, and a health impact assessor that translates resulting pollutant changes into monetized health damages. Across multiple regions in the United States, our health-driven optimization framework yields substantially lower prediction errors in terms of public health impacts than fuel mix-driven baselines. A case study on electric vehicle charging schedules illustrates the public health gains enabled by our method and the actionable guidance it can offer for health-informed energy management. Overall, this work shows how AI models can be explicitly designed to enable health-informed energy management for advancing public health and broader societal well-being. Our datasets and code are released at: https://github.com/Ren-Research/Health-Impact-Predictor.

articles.title: Variational analysis of determinantal varieties
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.22613v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Determinantal varieties---the sets of bounded-rank matrices or tensors---have attracted growing interest in low-rank optimization. The tangent cone to low-rank sets is widely studied and underpins a range of geometric methods. The second-order geometry, which encodes curvature information, is more intricate. In this work, we develop a unified framework to derive explicit formulas for both first- and second-order tangent sets to various low-rank sets, including low-rank matrices, tensors, symmetric matrices, and positive semidefinite matrices. The framework also accommodates the intersection of a low-rank set and another set satisfying some assumptions, thereby yielding a tangent intersection rule. Through the lens of tangent sets, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition under which a nonsmooth problem and its smooth parameterization share equivalent second-order stationary points. As applications, we exploit tangent sets to characterize optimality conditions for low-rank optimization and prove that verifying second-order optimality is NP-hard. Moreover, for low-rank semidefinite programs, the Burer--Monteiro parameterization maps fourth-order stationary points of the parameterized problem to second-order stationary points of the original problem. In a separate line of analysis, we investigate variational geometry of the graph of the normal cone to matrix varieties, deriving the explicit Bouligand tangent cone, Fr\'echet and Mordukhovich normal cones to the graph. These results are further applied to develop optimality conditions for low-rank bilevel programs.

articles.title: How Large Language Models Misrepresent American Climate Opinions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.23889v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate public opinion, standing in for survey respondents as "silicon samples." Whether they faithfully represent U.S. climate opinion, particularly at the intersections of race, gender, and ideology, remains largely untested. We prompted six large language models with the profiles of 978 respondents to a nationally representative U.S. climate opinion survey and compared the generated responses with those respondents' own answers across 20 questions. The models compress the diversity of American climate opinion, pulling predictions toward the population mean: less-concerned groups are predicted as more concerned, more-concerned groups as less, and the variance of predicted responses falls, on average, 29% below that of human responses. The compression is intersectional. The models apply one gender assumption, predicting women as more pro-climate than men in every racial group. The assumption matches the direction of the human pattern for White, Hispanic, and Other Americans and runs the wrong way for Black Americans. We claim the direction of that difference rather than its size, since it rests on small cells at the ideological extreme. An audit of gender alone would report that the models understate the gender gap, and would miss that the error changes direction by race, which is what single-variable audits cannot detect. What is at stake is not accuracy alone but representation: whose views a synthetic sample renders legible.

articles.title: The Post-Training Dilemma: Why We Should Rethink the Sequential SFT-RL Paradigm
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.07389v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This position paper argues that the sequential supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning (SFT-then-RL) pipeline---the de facto paradigm for large language model (LLM) post-training---has a fundamental property that cannot be fixed by hyperparameter tuning: SFT and RL optimize over nearly orthogonal parameter subspaces, so RL inevitably degrades the capabilities acquired during the preceding SFT phase. Under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition, which is empirically observed for over-parameterized networks, we show that RL increases the SFT loss by at least $\frac{\mu}{2}\mathrm{dist}(\theta_{\mathrm{RL}}, \Theta^*_{\mathrm{SFT}})^2$ for some $\mu>0$. Although the KL penalty can constrain distributional shift, it cannot correct the underlying gradient misalignment between the two objectives. Experiments on Qwen3-0.6B across four tasks confirm the theoretical predictions: on MATH-500, Alpaca, HH-RLHF, and SST-2, the SFT loss increases after the RL phase. We identify the underlying mechanism as persistent near-orthogonality between the gradients of the two objectives, paired with opposing landscape dynamics: SFT flattens the loss landscape while RL re-sharpens it. Based on our analysis, we propose three promising research directions: (1) joint optimization of the two objectives with gradient surgery to resolve conflicting updates; (2) landscape-aware scheduling that terminates RL training at the theoretically optimal point; and (3) characterizing the model scale threshold above which SFT becomes unnecessary.

articles.title: EMA Policy Gradient: Taming Reinforcement Learning for LLMs with EMA Anchor and Top-k KL
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.04417v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has enabled Large Language Models (LLMs) to acquire increasingly complex reasoning and agentic behaviors. In this work, we propose two simple techniques to improve policy gradient algorithms for LLMs. First, we replace the fixed anchor policy during RL with an Exponential Moving Average (EMA), similar to a target network in deep Q-learning. Second, we introduce Top-$k$ KL estimator, which allows for flexible interpolation between exact KL and sampled KL. We derive the stability conditions for using EMA anchor; moreover, we show that our Top-$k$ KL estimator yields both unbiased KL values and unbiased gradients at any $k$, while bringing the benefits of exact KL. When combined with GRPO, the two techniques (EMA-PG) lead to a significant performance boost. On math reasoning, it allows R1-distilled Qwen-1.5B to reach 53.9% on OlympiadBench compared to 50.8% by GRPO. On agentic RL domains, with Qwen-3B base, EMA-PG improves GRPO by an average of 35.6% across 7 datasets of Q&A with search engines, including 29.7% $\rightarrow$ 45.8% on HotpotQA, 27.4% $\rightarrow$ 40.5% on 2WikiMultiHopQA. Overall, we show that EMA-PG is a simple, principled, and powerful approach to scaling RL for LLMs. Code: https://github.com/LunjunZhang/ema-pg

articles.title: VLRS-Bench: A Vision-Language Reasoning Benchmark for Remote Sensing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.07045v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled complex reasoning. However, existing remote sensing (RS) benchmarks remain heavily biased toward perception tasks, such as object recognition and scene classification. This limitation hinders the development of MLLMs for cognitively demanding RS applications. To address this, we propose a Vision Language ReaSoning Benchmark (VLRS-Bench), which is the first benchmark exclusively dedicated to complex RS reasoning. Structured across the three core dimensions of Cognition, Decision, and Prediction, VLRS-Bench comprises 2,000 question-answer pairs with an average question length of 129.87 words, spanning 14 tasks and up to eight temporal phases. VLRS-Bench is constructed via a specialized pipeline that integrates RS-specific priors and expert knowledge to ensure geospatial realism and reasoning complexity. Experimental results reveal significant bottlenecks in existing state-of-the-art MLLMs, providing critical insights for advancing multimodal reasoning within the remote sensing community.

articles.title: On the Complexity of Offline Reinforcement Learning with Q*-Approximation and Partial Coverage
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.12107v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study offline reinforcement learning under $Q^\star$-approximation and partial coverage, a setting that motivates practical algorithms such as Conservative $Q$-Learning (CQL; Kumar et al., 2020) but has received limited theoretical attention. Our work is inspired by the following open question: "Are $Q^\star$-realizability and Bellman completeness sufficient for sample-efficient offline RL under partial coverage?"
  We answer in the negative via an information-theoretic lower bound. To identify additional structure that enables sample-efficient offline RL under partial coverage, we introduce a general decision-estimation framework, inspired by model-free decision-estimation coefficients (DEC) for online RL (Foster et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2025b). Our framework decomposes offline RL complexity into decision complexity and value estimation error. This allows modular study of both sub-problems. Our result not only unifies existing results (Chen and Jiang, 2022; Uehara et al., 2023), but further improves and generalizes them. On the decision complexity side, our improvement includes: the first $\epsilon^{-2}$ sample complexity bound for soft $Q$-learning under partial coverage that improves Uehara et al.'s (2023) $\epsilon^{-4}$ bound, the removal of the need for additional online interaction in the value-gap setting of Chen and Jiang (2022), and new learnable settings beyond the above two cases. On the value estimation side, we provide a new characterization of the role of Bellman completeness under partial coverage, and the first characterization of offline learnability for general low-Bellman-rank MDPs (Jiang et al., 2017; Du et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2021). The latter is a canonical online RL setting that has remained unexplored in offline RL except for special cases. As a side contribution, our techniques give the first analysis of CQL in the function approximation setting.

articles.title: Learning Object-Centric Spatial Reasoning for Sequential Manipulation in Cluttered Environments
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.02511v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Sequential manipulation in clutter requires selecting which objects to remove and determining how to manipulate them. Learning both decisions jointly can complicate training and make failures difficult to diagnose. We present Unveiler, a modular framework that separates scene reasoning and object selection from action execution through a discrete object-index interface. Its Spatial Relationship Encoder (SRE) selects the best object to grasp, while a separate Action Decoder generates orientation-discretized push-grasp actions. The SRE is trained in two stages: imitation learning from heuristic demonstrations, followed by search-based policy improvement using simulated object removals. This training procedure requires no real-robot training data and allows the SRE to be paired with a different execution policy. We evaluate Unveiler in PyBullet simulation and on a physical Dofbot-Pro. In real-robot experiments, it retrieves two occluded targets in the prescribed order in 90\% of scenes, compared with 20-30\% for the heuristic, GPT-4o, and the imitation-only variant. In PyBullet, Unveiler achieves the highest task-completion rate across all six clutter-density and occlusion conditions, reaching 90.0\% under full occlusion with 6-9 objects, compared with 67.5\% for the heuristic and 60.0\% for ThinkGrasp. These results demonstrate the potential of modular, object-centric spatial reasoning for sequential manipulation in clutter.

articles.title: xAppGen: LLM-driven Natural Language Programming for Agile xApp Development
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.18604v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Traditional RAN systems are closed and monolithic, stifling innovation. The openness and programmability enabled by Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) are envisioned to revolutionize cellular networks with control-plane applications--xApps. The development of xApps (typically by third-party developers), however, remains time-consuming and cumbersome, often requiring months of manual coding and integration, which hinders the roll-out of new functionalities in practice. To lower the barrier of xApp development for both developers and network operators, we present xAppGen, the first LLM-driven natural language programming framework for agile xApps that automates the entire xApp development pipeline. In a nutshell, xAppGen turns high-level user intents into swiftly deployable xApps within minutes, eliminating the need for manual coding or testing. To this end, AutORAN builds a fully automated xApp generation pipeline, which integrates multiple functional modules (from user requirement elicitation, AI/ML function design and validation, to xApp synthesis and deployment). We design, implement, and comprehensively evaluate xAppGen on representative xApp tasks. Results show xAppGen-generated xApps can achieve similar or even better performance than the best known hand-crafted baselines. xAppGen drastically accelerates the xApp development cycle (from user intent elicitation to roll-out), streamlining O-RAN innovation.

articles.title: {\lambda}Split: Self-Supervised Content-Aware Spectral Unmixing for Fluorescence Microscopy
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.23647v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In fluorescence microscopy, spectral unmixing aims to recover individual fluorophore concentrations from spectral images that capture mixed fluorophore emissions. Since classical methods operate pixel-wise and rely on least-squares fitting, their performance degrades with increasingly overlapping emission spectra and higher levels of noise, suggesting that a data-driven approach that can learn and utilize a structural prior might lead to improved results. Learning-based approaches for spectral imaging do exist, but they are either not optimized for microscopy data or are developed for very specific cases that are not applicable to fluorescence microscopy settings. To address this, we propose {\lambda}Split, a physics-informed deep generative model that learns a conditional distribution over concentration maps using a hierarchical Variational Autoencoder. A fully differentiable Spectral Mixer enforces consistency with the image formation process, while the learned structural priors enable state-of-the-art unmixing and implicit noise removal. We demonstrate {\lambda}Split on 3 real-world datasets that we synthetically cast into a total of 66 challenging spectral unmixing benchmarks. We compare our results against a total of 10 baseline methods, including classical methods and a range of learning-based methods. Our results consistently show competitive performance and improved robustness in high noise regimes, when spectra overlap considerably, or when the spectral dimensionality is lowered, making {\lambda}Split a new state-of-the-art for spectral unmixing of fluorescent microscopy data. Importantly, {\lambda}Split is compatible with spectral data produced by standard confocal microscopes, enabling immediate adoption without specialized hardware modifications.

articles.title: OpenTME: An Open Dataset of AI-powered H&E Tumor Microenvironment Profiles from TCGA
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.12075v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a central role in cancer progression, treatment response, and patient outcomes, yet large-scale, consistent, and quantitative TME characterization from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histopathology remains scarce. We introduce OpenTME, an open-access dataset of pre-computed TME profiles derived from 5,268 H&E-stained whole-slide images across ten cancer types (bladder, breast, colorectal, head and neck, liver, lung, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, and stomach cancer) from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). All outputs were generated using HETA (H&E Tissue Analysis), an AI-powered application built on the Atlas family of pathology foundation models, which performs tissue quality control, tissue segmentation, cell detection and classification, tumor zone and tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) detection, and spatial neighborhood analysis, yielding over 20,000 quantitative readouts per slide at cell-level resolution, including curated features such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, tumor mitotic index, or mature TLS counts. OpenTME is available for non-commercial academic research on Hugging Face. We will continue to expand OpenTME over time and anticipate it will serve as a resource for biomarker discovery, spatial biology research, and the development of computational methods for TME analysis.

articles.title: Beyond Visual Fidelity: Benchmarking Super-Resolution Models for Large-Scale Remote Sensing Imagery via Downstream Task Integration
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.00310v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Super-resolution (SR) techniques have made major advances in reconstructing high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs. The increased resolution provides visual enhancement and utility for monitoring tasks. In particular, SR has been increasingly developed for satellite-based Earth observation, with applications in urban planning, agriculture, ecology, and disaster response. However, existing SR studies and benchmarks typically use fidelity metrics such as PSNR or SSIM, whereas the true utility of super-resolved images lies in supporting downstream tasks such as land cover classification, biomass estimation, and change detection. To bridge this gap, we introduce GeoSR-Bench, a downstream task-integrated SR benchmark dataset to evaluate SR models beyond fidelity metrics. GeoSR-Bench comprises spatially co-located, temporally aligned, and quality-controlled image pairs from about 36,000 locations across diverse land covers, spanning resolutions from 500m to 0.6m. To the best of our knowledge, GeoSR-Bench is the first SR benchmark that directly connects improved image resolution from SR models with downstream Earth monitoring tasks, including land cover segmentation, infrastructure mapping, and biophysical variable estimation. Using GeoSR-Bench, we benchmark GAN, transformer, neural operator, and diffusion-based SR models on perceptual quality and downstream task performance. We conduct experiments with 270 settings, covering 2 cross-platform SR tasks, 9 SR models, 3 downstream task models, and 5 downstream tasks for each SR task. The results show that improvements in traditional SR metrics often do not correlate with gains in task performance, and the correlations can be negative, indicating that these metrics provide limited guidance for selecting superior models for downstream tasks. This reveals the need to integrate downstream tasks into SR model development and evaluation.

articles.title: Topology-Driven Anti-Entanglement Control for Soft Robots
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.05236v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In the field of precision manufacturing in complex constrained environments, the role of soft robots is increasingly prominent, and the realization of anti-winding control based on multi-intelligent body reinforcement learning has become a research hotspot. One of the core problems at present is to coordinate multiple robots to complete the unwinding operation in a highly constrained environment. The existing distributed training framework faces some observability challenges in high-density barrier and unstable environments, resulting in poor learning results. This paper proposes a topology-driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (TD-MARL) framework to coordinate multi-robot systems to avoid entanglement. Specifically, the critical network adopts centralized learning, so that each intelligent body can perceive the strategies of other intelligent bodies by sharing the topological state, thus alleviating the training instability caused by complex interactions; eliminating the demand for communication resources between robots through distributed execution, Upgrade system reliability; the integrated topological security layer uses topological invariants to accurately assess and mitigate the risk of entanglement to avoid the strategy from falling into local difficulties. Finally, the full simulation experiments carried out in the real simulation environment show that the method is better than the current advanced deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method in terms of convergence and anti-winding effect.

articles.title: Detecting AI-Generated Videos with Spiking Neural Networks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.05895v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern AI-generated videos are photorealistic at the single-frame level, leaving inter-frame dynamics as the main remaining axis for detection. Existing detectors typically handle this temporal evidence in three ways: feeding the full frame sequence to a generic temporal backbone, reducing one dominant temporal cue to fixed video-level descriptors, or comparing temporal features to real-video statistics through a detection metric. These strategies degrade sharply under cross-generator evaluation, where artifact type and timescale vary across generators. On caption-paired benchmark, GenVidBench, we identify two signatures that prior detectors do not jointly exploit: AI-generated videos exhibit smoother frame-to-frame temporal residuals at the pixel level, and more compact trajectories in the semantic feature space, indicating a temporal smoothness gap at both levels. We further observe that, when raw video is fed into a Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), fake clips elicit firing predominantly at object and motion boundaries, unlike real clips, suggesting that the SNN responds to temporal artifacts localized at edges. These cues are sparse, asynchronous, and concentrated at moments of change, which makes SNNs a natural choice for this task: their event-driven, sparsely-activated dynamics align with the structure of the residual signal in a way that dense ANN backbones do not. Building on this observation, we propose MAST, a detector that processes multi-channel temporal residuals with a spike-driven temporal branch alongside a frozen semantic encoder for cross-generator generalization. On the GenVideo benchmark, MAST achieves 93.14\% mean accuracy across 10 unseen generators under strict cross-generator evaluation, matching or surpassing the strongest ANN-based detectors and demonstrating the practical applicability of SNNs to AI-generated video detection.

articles.title: The Endogeneity of Miscalibration: Impossibility and Escape in Scored Reporting
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.07671v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: An agent's probability report is paid for twice: by a strictly proper scoring rule, which rewards accuracy, and by an approval rule for the decision it triggers. An approval rule that is not affine is known to defeat truthful reporting. We show the conflict is built in: whenever perfect screening is attainable, the welfare-maximizing approval rule is never affine. The distortion is predictable: there is a reserve report at which pretending to be the marginal type costs exactly what approval is worth. Approving every report at or above the reserve sorts agents as if their beliefs were observed, under every strictly proper score and for any belief distribution. So does a continuous rule with one corner; under strict feasibility no continuously differentiable rule does. The binding constraint is steepness, not smoothness: a slope-capped rule sorts perfectly if and only if the cap reaches the critical slope, the steepest chord of the pretending cost up to the reserve; below it the welfare loss is cubic in the shortfall. For the Brier, log and power scores, and whenever the pretending cost is convex up to the reserve, the critical slope has a closed form. The instances are AI-agent oversight and marketplace operation.

articles.title: Behavioral Integrity Verification for AI Agent Skills
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.11770v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Agent skills extend LLM agents with privileged third-party capabilities such as filesystem access, credentials, network calls, and shell execution. Existing safety work catches malicious prompts and risky runtime actions, but the skill artifact itself goes unverified. We formalize this as the behavioral integrity verification (BIV) problem: a typed set comparison between declared and actual capabilities over a shared taxonomy that bridges code, instructions, and metadata. The BIV framework instantiates this comparison by pairing deterministic code analysis with LLM-assisted capability extraction. The resulting structured evidence supports three downstream analyses: deviation taxonomy, root-cause classification, and malicious-skill detection. On 49,943 skills from the OpenClaw registry, the deviation taxonomy reveals a pervasive description-implementation gap: 80.0% of skills have at least one deviation in the taxonomy, with four compound-threat categories surfaced. Root-cause classification finds that deviations are mostly oversight, not malice: 81.1% trace to developer oversight and 18.9% to adversarial intent, with 5.0% of skills carrying predicted multi-stage attack chains. On a 906-skill malicious-skill detection benchmark, BIV reaches an F1 of 0.949, outperforming state-of-the-art rule-based and single-pass LLM baselines. These results demonstrate behavioral integrity auditing for agent skills at scale.

articles.title: Spectral Vision Transformer for Efficient Tokenization with Limited Data
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.12026v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vision transformers tokenize an image into patches, which couples the token count to resolution and requires the embedding to be learned from data. We propose a spectral vision transformer architecture for efficient tokenization in the limited-data regime, with an emphasis on medical imaging. Rather than using spatial patches, we tokenize into coefficients of a fixed basis. This approach defines each token as one spectral mode, and the sequence length is chosen rather than implied by resolution, reducing the cost of attention. Our proposed spectral ViT shows superior or comparable performance where data is scarce in public medical imaging benchmarks, natural images, object shapes, simulations, and protected clinical data. We release our code at: https://github.com/agr78/SpectralViT.

articles.title: Authors' Response to AI-Based Reviews: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.16623v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Background: Large language models are increasingly used to assist scholarly peer review, but there is limited evidence about how authors judge their feedback and use it to revise their papers.
  Methods: We studied authors' experiences of receiving an auxiliary AI review alongside human reviews in three computer-science cohorts: LifeCLEF 2025, LifeCLEF 2026, and CVWW 2026. Post-review questionnaires yielded 92 responses concerning 71 papers. We summarized closed-ended answers using descriptive statistics and examined free-text responses through thematic analysis.
  Results: Most responses rated the AI review useful (82/92 (89%), and 82/92 (89%) reported using at least some of its suggestions in revision. Authors reported that AI identified issues missed by human reviewers ((76/92 (83%). However, 44/92 (48%) trusted AI feedback less than human feedback, and 58/92 (63%) reported incorrect or misleading comments. Authors valued suggestions that improved clarity and reproducibility, but also described overlooked evidence, inappropriate demands, and difficulty finding useful comments within lengthy reviews. They emphasized the need to check AI feedback and retain control over how their manuscripts were processed. Future review by both humans and AI was supported by 85/92 (92%); 83/92 (90%) preferred advance notice and 73/92 (79%) supported explicit consent.
  Conclusions: Authors often found AI reviews useful for revision without trusting them as much as human reviews. These exploratory findings favor a supplementary role for AI, with human oversight, clear disclosure, and author consent. They do not establish that AI can replace human reviewers or improve manuscript quality.

articles.title: Channel-wise Vector Quantization: Native 1D Visual Tokenization with Learnable Ordering
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.26089v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We present Channel-wise Vector Quantization (CVQ), a novel image tokenization paradigm that replaces patch-wise tokens with channel-wise tokens. Unlike conventional vector quantization, which assigns a discrete token to each patch feature vector, CVQ quantizes each channel of the feature map. This represents an image as a 1D channel sequence with learnable coarse-to-fine ordering, rather than a 2D patch grid. Based on CVQ, we introduce a new visual autoregressive framework with "next-channel prediction". Instead of rendering images patch by patch in raster order, our Channel-wise Autoregressive (CAR) model predicts image channels sequentially, producing progressively enriched visual details. Specifically, it first sketches global structure and then refines fine-grained attributes, akin to a human artist's workflow. Empirically, we show that: (1) CVQ exhibits strong codebook scalability, maintaining 95%+ utilization with up to $2^{16}$ entries while delivering growing reconstruction gains over VQ as the codebook scales up; and (2) CAR attains a DPG score of 86.7 and a GenEval score of 0.79, demonstrating strong effectiveness for text-to-image generation.

articles.title: Learning Which Evidence-Seeking Decisions Matter: Calibrated Counterfactual Replay for Language Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.05263v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Language agents answer questions by searching, reading, and checking claims. A reward on the final answer says little about which of those decisions earned it, since an agent can reach the right string after redundant searches or with half the evidence missing. We treat the question as an experiment. At a saved decision point, PCCC-RL, for prefix-conditioned counterfactual credit, restores the tool state, runs the action the agent chose alongside a feasible alternative, and lets the same frozen policy finish both branches. The difference in final score then samples what the decision was worth. Replaying everything is too expensive, so the method predicts each action's credit up front, checks a random subset, and uses the recorded selection probabilities to correct the errors of that prediction, spending the budget where a further check can still move the training signal. Alternatives are drawn from the prefix alone, which keeps the comparison a usable gradient baseline. On HotpotQA and MuSiQue, joint exact match, requiring a correct answer together with complete supporting evidence, reaches 56.71% and 36.82%, gains of 4.19 and 3.86 points over a baseline with the same replay access. The gain concentrates in complete evidence chains and accumulates over many updates. Single-update effects stay uncertain, and citation coverage and scope distinctions such as "none" versus "not all" remain open.

articles.title: DAST: A VLM-LLM Framework for Cross-Interface Anomaly Detection in O-RAN
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.06261v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: O-RAN enables a disaggregated baseband stack with programmable functions that communicate over standardized open interfaces. The same openness that enables multi-vendor composition also expands the attack surface across logically decoupled tiers that make up the compute continuum. Among these threats, Denial-of-Service and performance-degradation attacks, which account for the majority of catalogued O-RAN threats, are particularly difficult to detect. Traditional Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) methods fail in this new regime where labelled baselines are scarce, threats evolve faster than detectors can be retrained, and the high-dimensional multivariate telemetry overwhelms monolithic inference models. To address these challenges, we present DAST, a zero-shot multi-agent framework for cross-interface anomaly detection in O-RAN that chains a three-stage VLM $\rightarrow$ LLM $\rightarrow$ VLM pipeline. DAST converts multivariate KPI streams into visual representations, scores textual per-interface descriptions against O-RAN domain knowledge, and verifies suspects on high-resolution heatmaps to output the problematic interfaces, the anomalous time intervals, an indicative O-RAN WG11-aligned operational impact rating and the decision rationale. We evaluate DAST on real network traces collected from an O-RAN testbed under representative performance degradation scenarios, achieving 0.910 F1-Score and 0.843 Accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art TSAD baselines.

articles.title: The Montparnasse Algorithm for RNA Design
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.07562v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Inverse RNA Folding consists of finding a nucleotide sequence that folds into a predefined secondary structure. It is useful for synthetic biology, medicine, and nanotechnology. We propose Montparnasse, a Monte Carlo search framework based on Generalized Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation, augmented with a structural prior derived from the energy model, slow and long adaptation at level 1, a lexicographic multicriteria evaluation, a local repair of the pairs the predicted folding gets wrong, and a fleet of parallel workers coupled through a shared beam whose diversity is maintained on the faults the candidates make rather than on the candidates themselves. On the Eterna100 V1 benchmark, with both solvers folding through the same ViennaRNA 1.8.5 library under the Turner 1999 model, with 100 parallel workers and a budget of 30 minutes per puzzle, Montparnasse solves a median of 96 of the 100 puzzles against a median of 90 for DesiRNA, the previous state of the art, each figure taken over five passes. It is faster on 88 of the 90 puzzles that both solve, with a median solving time of 0.9 s against 5.6 s, and it solves 55 puzzles within the first second. The one puzzle no pass reaches is solved under the same model with a longer budget, so every Eterna100 V1 target is solved by Montparnasse.

articles.title: SPACE: Source-free Proxy Anchor Concept Erasure for MLLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.09868v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face growing privacy risks and regulatory constraints, machine unlearning (MU) has emerged as a crucial solution for removing sensitive data while preserving model performance. However, existing MU methods typically rely on visual data of the target concepts, which is often unavailable due to strict data retention policies, thus creating a demand for source-free unlearning approaches that operate without access to the target data. In this work, we propose Source-free Proxy Anchor Concept Erasure (SPACE), the first source-free unlearning framework specialized for MLLMs. SPACE consists of two stages: (1) Text-Guided Proxy Anchor Selection (TPAS), which retrieves semantically aligned proxy anchors from the shared feature space. (2) Dual-Constraint Semantic Isolation (DCSI), which optimizes these anchors to indirectly erase target concepts. DCSI confines updates to the null space of retained knowledge, ensuring structural integrity. We theoretically prove that SPACE strictly bounds the perturbation on retained knowledge and maximizes feature spectral entropy, thereby maintaining the model's performance. Furthermore, extensive experiments across six datasets show that SPACE achieves performance comparable to that of state-of-the-art data-dependent methods, validating its effectiveness in source-free MU scenarios. The source code will be released.

articles.title: Implicit Neural Representations of Individual Behavior
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.12200v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study policy representation learning from unlabeled multi-policy behavioral data. Each episode is generated by a fixed policy, but policy labels are unavailable. This setting appears in robotics play, demonstrations, games, racing, and other datasets where heterogeneous behaviors are mixed without annotations. We introduce Behavioral INR, a self-supervised generative model that adapts implicit neural representations (INRs) from vision to behavior. Instead of mapping coordinates to RGB values, Behavioral INR represents a policy as a state-action function mapping states to subsequent actions. An episode-level latent modulates this function through FiLM layers, yielding a generative prior over policies and allowing policy identity to be inferred without supervision. Because INRs treat each datapoint as samples from an underlying function, the same model naturally accommodates variable episode lengths and different sampling granularities, as in vision INRs with different image resolutions. We also define policy-level out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts along state-distribution and action-distribution axes, which arise when policies overlap in states or actions but are not captured by standard behavioral OOD settings based only on new agents or environments. We evaluate on synthetic Gaussian random field data, MuJoCo demonstrations with controlled OOD splits, and real-world chess, Formula 1 racing, robotics, and Seek-Avoid datasets. Behavioral INR most consistently improves policy identifiability in the hardest continuous state-action settings, especially when longer episodes, more policies, and OOD splits reduce the usefulness of marginal shortcuts; amortized history encoders remain competitive when policy identity can be recovered from symbolic repetition or low-dimensional action statistics.

articles.title: Rational Sparse Autoencoder
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.14990v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are standard tools for mechanistic interpretability, but current SAE families are constrained by fixed encoder nonlinearities such as ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. This hard-codes a particular sparsity mechanism into the model and can distort the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off. We introduce the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function. The design is motivated by a reconstruction advantage that we prove for RSAE at matched expected sparsity, with guaranteed non-inferiority to ReLU and, under stated assumptions, provable improvements over JumpReLU and TopK. The model is then implemented through a two-stage pipeline: an initialization procedure that copies the pre-trained baseline SAE weights and calibrates the scale parameters along with the rational coefficients; followed by a fine-tuning step under a sparsity-regularized reconstruction objective that holds $\ell_0$ at the teacher's value. Consistent with this theory, on residual-stream activations of three open-weight language models and across all three baseline activation families, the RSAE improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity. These gains are consistent across host language models, across baseline activation families, and across the full range of baseline sparsity we tested, while the upgrade itself adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and one training run takes between about 4 and 25 minutes on a single consumer GPU.

articles.title: When Does Depth Matter For In-Context Learning? Adaptive Inference in Deep Transformers
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.16694v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transformers perform computations through many successive attention and feedforward blocks, allowing them to learn complex correlations between a large collection of coupled variables. When does stacking successive attention-feedforward computations over many layers provide a computational advantage over a single transformer block? We address this question by examining in-context learning in generalized linear attention transformers. We first introduce a general theory of distributed inference in such transformers, subject to constraints on communication and depth. We show that such systems can exploit internal representations (`function vectors') to infer a latent context variable at increasingly finer scales over its layers. For an in-context linear regression task, the theory predicts that while one-layer transformers without feedforward blocks are optimal for Gaussian priors over the context variable, multi-layer transformers are superior for non-Gaussian, tree-like priors. Trained linear attention transformers reproduce quantitative predictions from the theory. Using causal key-patching experiments, we verify that function vectors in intermediate layers mediate adaptive routing of information. Our results suggest that depth and feedforward blocks enable transformers to implement adaptive inference, and this is advantageous when the distribution over latent variables has hierarchical structure.

articles.title: Random coloured digraphs defined by a Markov logic network
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.23715v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A Markov Logic Network (MLN) $M$ is a probabilistic relational model used in Statistical Relational Artificial Intelligence for defining a probability distribution $P_D^M$ on the set $W_D$ of possible worlds with domain $D$ for an arbitrary finite domain $D$. An MLN consists of first-order formulas, which we call soft constraints, with associated weights which are nonnegative real numbers. The behaviour of the probability distribution, including the effect of the weights, on different domain sizes is poorly understood. We approach the problem in a systematic way by studying sequences $(P_n^M(\psi) : n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots)$ where $\psi$ is a first-order sentence and $P_n^M(\psi)$ is the probability that $\psi$ holds in $W_D$ where $D = [n] := \{1, \ldots, n\}$. We consider a first-order language that can express a property $P(x)$ and relation $R(x, y)$ and show that all of the following cases can be realized for an MLN $M$ such that each of its soft constraints is a boolean combination of $P(x)$, $P(y)$ and $R(x, y)$ in which both $x$ and $y$ appears:  For every first-order sentence $\psi$, $P_n^M(\psi)$ converges to 0 or 1 as $n\to\infty$. For every first-order sentence $\psi$, $P_n^M(\psi)$ converges as $n\to\infty$ but not necessarily to 0 or 1. There is a first-order sentence $\psi$ such that $P_n^M(\psi)$ does not converge as $n\to\infty$. In fact, all three cases can be realized even after fixing the soft constraints and, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, by varying their weights by less than $\varepsilon$. We also show that, given any MLN as described above, we can efficiently determine which case it belongs to by inspecting the MLN. Then we show that if the weights are scaled by $1/n$ then we end up in case~(1) no matter how the weights are chosen.

articles.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.28666v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Agent-based AI has enabled the automation of tasks by exposing application tools and resources to large language models (LLMs). However, to improve scope and accuracy, agents are often given access rights that exceed those of ordinary users, introducing significant security risks and potential regulatory breaches. This paper applies the AI Trust, Risk, and Security Management (TRiSM) framework to a medical report-generation application to demonstrate how an insecure baseline workflow can be transformed into a security-conscious agentic workflow. Both designs were evaluated with five LLMs (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash) across 800 report generations and 500 attack trials covering RAG poisoning, data-field injection and client-side network injection. The redesign reduced attack success from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection (McNemar p < 0.001 for both), removed network injection by construction, and raised report accuracy from 72.5% to 86.5%. In an exploratory post-hoc grouping by attack goal, success against attacks aimed outside the report task, such as data disclosure and tool abuse, fell from 21.7% to 2.5% and no patient record was disclosed under the redesign. Attacks altering the reported Covid-19 diagnosis remained effective, accounting for 32 of the 35 successful attacks against the redesign.
